concepts.def: Roman tragedies of Seneca (1st c. CE) — declamatory, violent, full of ghosts and revenge; deeply influential on Elizabethan drama.
Elizabethan/Jacobean genre (Kyd's Spanish Tragedy, Hamlet) featuring a ghost, a wronged hero and bloody resolution.
Five-act tragic structure focusing on a noble protagonist's fall through internal flaw and external pressure.
A high-status protagonist whose fall arouses pity and fear; often noble but flawed.
Excessive pride that brings down the tragic hero — Greek concept distinct from but related to hamartia.
Exposition, complication, climax, falling action, catastrophe — the standard Shakespearean arc.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Seneca's tragedies were probably written for recitation rather than full performance. They feature long declamations, gore, ghosts and rhetorical excess.

Their influence on Elizabethan revenge drama — through Kyd to Shakespeare — is direct and visible.

Thomas Kyd's Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587) established the revenge formula: ghost demands vengeance, hero delays, play-within-a-play, bloody finale.

Hamlet sits squarely in this tradition while transcending it through psychological depth.
The five-act structure provides a familiar arc. Act III usually contains the climax (Macbeth's murder, Hamlet's play); the catastrophe arrives in Act V.
